dais.definition: a raised platform for a speaker or seat of honor
sentences: The guests on the dais could see everything and hear almost nothing.
A dais raises the speaker eighteen inches and the stakes considerably.

dalliance.definition: a brief casual romance or idle dawdling
sentences: A brief dalliance with modern art left him with two canvases and no explanation.
The dalliance cost him a marriage and a rather good house.

damp.definition: to dull or lessen the force of
sentences: The rain damped the crowd's enthusiasm without reducing its size.
Good springs damp the shock; bad news damps everything else.
The dapper little man in the corner turned out to own the entire building.
Dapper at seventy, he still had his shoes made by the same shop.
The size of the archive daunted three researchers and delighted the fourth.
Nothing daunted her except the telephone.
The reading list was daunting until she realized half of it was footnotes.
A daunting task shrinks the moment somebody starts it in front of you.

dawdle.definition: to waste time; to move slowly
sentences: He dawdled over the first page for a week and wrote the rest in two days.
Children dawdle on the way to school and sprint home, which is a whole philosophy.
There was no dearth of opinions and a striking dearth of evidence.
The word is a cousin of "dear": scarcity is what makes things expensive.
The launch was a debacle: two crashes, one apology, and a resignation by Friday.
Every debacle has a moment where somebody could have said stop.

debase.definition: to lower in quality, value, or dignity
sentences: Rome debased its coinage until the silver was mostly optimism.
He debased the award by giving it to donors.
A debased currency buys the same bread at four times the price.
The debased version of the story kept the scandal and lost the point.
A weekend of debauchery cost him a job he had wanted for six years.
The emperor's debauchery is better documented than his administration, which is unfair to both.
A debilitating fever kept her from the trial she had spent two years preparing.
Debilitating doubt is harder to treat than any of the certainties it replaces.
Debonair in a borrowed jacket, he talked his way into the reception.
The word once meant "of good disposition" and has since acquired a tuxedo.

debunk.definition: to expose as false or exaggerated
sentences: The myth was debunked in 1957 and appears in three textbooks printed last year.
Debunking travels at half the speed of the claim it corrects.

debutante.definition: a young woman formally entering society
sentences: The debutante ball survived two wars and finally died of embarrassment.
She was presented as a debutante in June and was organizing a strike by October.
Every generation diagnoses decadence in the one that follows it.
The empire's decadence was described enthusiastically by historians who had never visited.

decadent.definition: self-indulgent to the point of moral decline
sentences: A decadent dessert menu is a marketing category; a decadent age is a verdict.
The decadent poets took the insult as a name and wore it beautifully.
A jet at takeoff reaches 140 decibels, which is the point where sound becomes injury.
Decibels are logarithmic: ten more is ten times the energy, not ten percent more noise.

decimate.definition: to destroy a large portion of
sentences: The blight decimated the orchards and the argument about the word decimate.
Roman legions decimated mutinous units by killing one man in ten, chosen by lot.

decimation.definition: destruction of a large part of something
sentences: The decimation of the fishery took nine years and one very efficient trawler design.
Decimation of the archive was accidental, which made it no less permanent.

decipher.definition: to make out the meaning of something obscure
sentences: It took nine months to decipher a shopping list written in shorthand.
Linear B was deciphered by an architect in his spare time, which infuriated the professionals.
He declaimed against the budget for forty minutes and voted for it.
Declaiming is what speaking becomes when the speaker can hear himself.
The path ended in a declivity too steep for the cart and too long to carry.
Acclivity goes up, declivity goes down, and both are usually called "the hill."
A decorous silence followed the announcement, broken by one very audible laugh.
Decorous behavior at a funeral is a performance everybody agrees to give.
Decorum required a black tie; the emergency required running.
Parliamentary decorum forbids calling someone a liar, so members have invented forty phrases meaning it.

decree.definition: an official order with legal force
sentences: The decree arrived by fax and abolished a department of two hundred.
By decree the calendar lost eleven days, and riots followed over the missing time.
Editorials decried the decision all week and none proposed an alternative.
He decried waste in a speech that cost forty thousand to stage.

deduce.definition: to reach a conclusion by reasoning
sentences: From a tan line and a train ticket she deduced the whole holiday.
Holmes claimed to deduce; usually he was inferring, which is less impressive and more useful.
The letter was deemed inappropriate by a committee that never quite said why.
What one century deems genius the next deems a phase.
Someone defaced the portrait with a mustache that historians now defend as period-appropriate.
Defacing a banknote is illegal, which has stopped precisely nobody.

default.definition: failure to fulfill an obligation; a preset option
sentences: The country's default in 2001 rewrote every textbook chapter on sovereign debt.
Nobody changes the default setting, which is why defaults are the most powerful design decision.

defer.definition: to postpone, or to yield to another's judgment
sentences: They deferred the decision twice and inherited it a third time, unchanged.
She deferred to the surgeon on medicine and to nobody at all on grammar.
Out of deference to the family, the report withheld two names.
Deference to expertise is wisdom; deference to seniority is often just furniture.
His deferential manner disappeared the moment the contract was signed.
A deferential junior asks the question everyone senior was afraid to.
She deflected the question with a joke and answered a different one entirely.
The shield deflected the blow; the argument deflected the blame.
A small grant defrayed the travel and none of the actual research.
Ticket sales defrayed about a third of what the festival cost.
A deft edit removed two hundred words and improved every remaining one.
Deft hands and a bad temper made him the best and least popular repairman in town.
The deftness of her reply left the interviewer with nowhere to go.
Deftness looks like ease and is made entirely of repetition.

degrade.definition: to reduce in quality, status, or dignity
sentences: Plastic degrades over centuries, which is a fact best considered before opening the packet.
The policy degraded the service and was reported as an efficiency.
Fans deified the coach in October and demanded his dismissal in March.
Rome deified emperors after death, which was cheaper than doing so while they lived.

deign.definition: to do something considered beneath one's dignity
sentences: He finally deigned to answer the email, three weeks and one lawsuit later.
She did not deign to reply, which was itself an eloquent reply.
The verdict dejected everyone except the lawyer, who had planned for it.
Nothing dejects a team faster than a leader who has already given up.

delegate.definition: to entrust a task to another
sentences: He could not delegate, so he worked eighty hours and everyone else worked twenty.
Delegate the task, not the blame.
The deleterious effects showed up eight years after the product was discontinued.
Constant interruption is more deleterious to thought than outright noise.
The jury deliberated for nine days over evidence that took two hours to present.
As an adjective it means intentional; as a verb, taking your time about it.

delicacy.definition: fineness or tact; a choice food
sentences: The matter required delicacy, so naturally it was handled by memo.
One country's delicacy is another's evidence of something having gone badly wrong.
The treaty delimited the border and left the river to change its mind annually.
First delimit the question, or the answer will keep growing.
The memo delineated four responsibilities and assigned all of them to one person.
She delineated the character in three sentences and the plot never caught up.
The delusion that everyone reads the appendix has ruined many careful reports.
A delusion held by one person is madness; held by a crowd, it is a market.

delve.definition: to research or dig into deeply
sentences: She delved into the parish records and emerged with an entirely different family.
Delve first meant to dig with a spade, which research still resembles.

demagogue.definition: a leader who exploits popular fears
sentences: A demagogue offers a villain where a statesman offers a budget.
The word means "leader of the people," which is how every demagogue introduces himself.

demarcate.definition: to mark boundaries or separate clearly
sentences: A single hedge demarcated two counties, three parishes, and one very long feud.
Science and pseudoscience are hard to demarcate, which is why philosophers still have jobs.
He would not demean himself by answering the accusation, which everyone read as guilt.
The job did not demean her; the way it was described did.

demonstrable.definition: able to be proven or shown
sentences: A demonstrable improvement in three metrics is worth more than a compelling story.
The claim was demonstrable, which is why nobody bothered demonstrating it.
He was undemonstrative for sixty years and wept openly at a dog's funeral.
A demonstrative greeting from a colleague usually means bad news is close behind.
Nothing demoralizes a team like watching a good idea die in committee.
The siege was designed to demoralize rather than destroy, which took longer and cost less.
She demurred at the price and accepted the terms.
He demurred, coughed, and then agreed to everything anyway.
Her demure reply concealed the fact that she had already bought the company.
Demure in public and ferocious in committee, she got everything she asked for.

denigrate.definition: to criticize unfairly; to blacken a reputation
sentences: He denigrated the work publicly and borrowed its method quietly.
The Latin root means to blacken, which is exactly what the gossip was for.
A red flag on the beach denotes danger; a red face denotes something else entirely.
Words denote their dictionary meaning and connote everything they have been used for.

denouement.definition: the final resolution of a plot
sentences: The denouement explained everything and satisfied nobody.
French for "untying": the plot is a knot, and the denouement undoes it.
He denounced the deal from the podium and signed a version of it in June.
To denounce is to condemn with an audience present; without one it is just grumbling.

dense.definition: thick and compact; hard to understand
sentences: The chapter is dense in the good way: nothing wasted, everything load-bearing.
Dense fog and dense prose share the property of hiding what is directly ahead.

deportment.definition: the way a person behaves or carries themselves
sentences: Her deportment under cross-examination impressed the jury more than her answers.
Schools once graded deportment, which was a polite word for sitting still.

depose.definition: to remove from office; to testify under oath
sentences: The king was deposed by a committee that met in a stable.
She was deposed for eleven hours and contradicted herself twice.
Every new medium has been accused of depraving the young, from novels to radio.
The censor claimed the play would deprave audiences who had already read the book.
The court described the crime's depravity in language usually reserved for weather.
Depravity requires effort; ordinary selfishness manages fine on its own.

deprecate.definition: to express disapproval of; to belittle
sentences: He deprecated his own contribution so persistently that people believed him.
Programmers deprecate a feature to warn you it is about to disappear.

depredation.definition: an act of plundering or destruction
sentences: Centuries of depredation left the temple with three columns and a very good story.
The depredations of damp did more damage to the library than any war.
The derelict warehouse became flats, then a landmark, then flats again.
Derelict in his duty, the guard had been asleep for the entire robbery.
Critics derided the design for a decade and now call it visionary.
It is easy to deride an idea and hard to build a better one.
The proposal was met with derision and adopted, quietly, four years later.
Derision is the cheapest form of criticism and the hardest to answer.
A derisive snort from the back row ended the presentation early.
The derisive nickname stuck for thirty years and outlived everyone who had meant it unkindly.
The album is derivative, competent, and completely unnecessary.
Every style looks derivative until enough time passes to call it a tradition.

derive.definition: to obtain or trace from a source
sentences: Half the vocabulary derives from Latin and pretends otherwise.
She derives more satisfaction from the footnotes than from the argument.
The figure is derived, not measured, which the headline declined to mention.
A derived unit like the newton is built from ones you can actually feel.
A derogative aside in the margin was the only comment the manuscript received.
The nickname was derogative in 1890 and is now printed on the school crest.

descry.definition: to catch sight of something distant
sentences: From the tower they descried a sail an hour before it mattered.
One can descry, in the early drafts, the shape of the book it became.

desecrate.definition: to treat something sacred with disrespect
sentences: The tomb was desecrated by looters who left the gold and took the inscriptions.
To desecrate is to undo a consecration, which apparently takes far less time.
The wind desiccated the topsoil until the fields simply blew away.
Bureaucracy can desiccate a good idea without ever formally rejecting it.
The desiccated flower fell out of the book intact after ninety years.
His prose was accurate, thorough, and desiccated past the point of readability.
Speed was desirable; accuracy was the desideratum.
The great desideratum of the field is a dataset nobody has yet been willing to fund.
Despair arrives quietly, usually disguised as being realistic.
He was the despair of his teachers and the delight of his readers.
He did it in despite of every instruction he had been given.
Now almost always a preposition, despite once meant the contempt itself.

despoil.definition: to plunder or strip of possessions
sentences: The coast was despoiled by developers who named the streets after what they removed.
Armies despoil; committees merely deplete.
History remembers the despoiler and forgets the archivist who saved the rest.
Every despoiler of a landscape has a brochure explaining why it was necessary.

despot.definition: a ruler with absolute, oppressive power
sentences: The despot built a road, a dam, and nine thousand statues of himself.
Enlightened despot is a term historians use when the roads were good.
The department was run on despotic lines by a man with no formal authority whatsoever.
Despotic rule is efficient right up until the succession.
He died destitute in a rented room and is now on the currency.
The argument was destitute of evidence and rich in adjectives.
A desultory search of the attic turned up three lamps and no will.
The word comes from a circus rider leaping between horses — motion without a route.
Her detached account of the disaster was the only readable one published that year.
A surgeon must be detached; a witness usually cannot manage it.
He described his own bankruptcy with the detachment of a weather report.
Detachment is a virtue in a judge and a warning sign in a friend.

detente.definition: an easing of hostility between rivals
sentences: The detente lasted four years and one particularly badly worded press release.
Detente between the two departments began, as usual, with a shared enemy.
Higher fines deterred nobody; visible enforcement deterred everybody.
Rain deterred the fair-weather protesters and revealed who was serious.
Postcode remains the strongest determinant of outcomes, which is an indictment of everything else.
The determinant was not talent but timing, as it usually is.
The lock is not a deterrent to a professional and works fine on everyone else.
The best deterrent is the belief you will be caught, not the size of the penalty.

detraction.definition: the act of belittling or disparaging
sentences: The review was three columns of detraction and one grudging final line.
Detraction subtracts: the word admits exactly what it does.
The delay was detrimental to the patient and convenient for the schedule.
Detrimental effects appear in the appendix; benefits appear on the cover.
Sociologists study deviance and discover mostly that societies enjoy defining it.
Yesterday's deviance is today's subculture and tomorrow's advertisement.

deviate.definition: to depart from an established course
sentences: The pilot deviated from the route by six miles and avoided the storm entirely.
He never deviated from the recipe, which is why the cake was never memorable.
A deviation of two degrees put the ship on the wrong side of the island.
Standard deviation measures how much reality wanders from its own average.

device.definition: a tool, or a scheme or technique
sentences: The unreliable narrator is a device, not an accident.
Left to his own devices, he built a boat in the garden and never sailed it.

devolve.definition: to transfer power downward; to degenerate
sentences: Powers devolved to the regions and the budget stayed exactly where it was.
The debate devolved into an argument about who had said what in 2011.
The puzzle was diabolic: solvable, elegant, and designed to waste your evening.
A diabolic plan requires a level of organization most villains cannot sustain.
The weather was diabolical, the pitch was worse, and the match went ahead anyway.
His diabolical timing meant the resignation landed during the annual gala.
The diadem was sold in 1923 and bought back by the museum for forty times the price.
A diadem signals sovereignty; a hat signals weather.
Diaphanous curtains turned the harsh afternoon into something almost kind.
Her argument was diaphanous: you could see straight through it, beautifully.
The letter began as a correction and became a diatribe by the second page.
A diatribe convinces nobody and relieves the author enormously.

dichotomy.definition: a division into two opposed parts
sentences: The nature-versus-nurture dichotomy has survived a century of evidence that it is false.
Most dichotomies are arguments that stopped looking for a third option.
Geography dictated the route long before engineers were consulted.
He dictated terms to a room that had already decided to refuse them.
His dictatorial editing produced a superb magazine and a permanent staffing crisis.
Dictatorial leadership works until somebody has to think without being told.
The old dictum that form follows function has been quoted by everyone who ignores it.
A judge's dictum is not binding, which does not stop lawyers from citing it.
The novel is didactic to the point of lecturing, and it sold four million copies.
Aesop is didactic; the fables survive anyway because the animals are funny.
Nothing differentiated the two proposals except the letterhead.
Wine experts can differentiate vintages; the rest of us can differentiate red from white.
Her diffidence in meetings hid a mind three steps ahead of the discussion.
Diffidence cost him the promotion; competence eventually got it back.
The diffident candidate answered brilliantly and apologized for doing so.
Diffident about his singing and fearless about everything else, he made an odd impression.
The argument is diffuse: good ideas scattered across sixty pages of throat-clearing.
Diffuse light flatters everyone, which is why photographers spend so much on it.

digress.definition: to depart from the main subject
sentences: He digressed for twenty minutes about a boat and somehow made the point better.
If I may digress — a sentence that guarantees the digression is already planned.

digression.definition: a temporary departure from the main topic
sentences: The book's best chapter is a digression about a bridge that never got built.
Two hours of digression left eleven minutes for the actual decision.
The dilapidated pier was condemned, photographed, and put on every postcard.
The Latin root involves stones falling off, which is exactly the image.

dilate.definition: to widen or expand; to speak at length
sentences: Pupils dilate in the dark and in the presence of someone you like, unhelpfully.
He dilated upon the subject until the audience dilated toward the exits.

dilatory.definition: tending to delay; slow to act
sentences: Dilatory tactics kept the case out of court for six years.
The dilatory reply arrived after the problem had solved itself.
A dilettante in six fields, he was interesting at dinner and useless on deadline.
The word once meant simply a lover of art; contempt was added later.
Diligent checking caught an error that would have cost a year's work.
The diligent student and the brilliant one meet at the same finish line, differently tired.
The diminutive conductor was invisible behind the score and audible three streets away.
A diminutive ending like "-let" makes a book a booklet and a pig a piglet.
The din of the market made conversation an act of shouting and faith.
Above the din, one voice asked the only useful question of the evening.
The dingy office produced the decade's most elegant mathematics.
One coat of paint took the room from dingy to merely plain.

dint.definition: force or means, as in "by dint of"
sentences: By dint of sheer repetition he learned every irregular verb in the language.
The word survives in one phrase and nowhere else, like a fossil in amber.

dirge.definition: a mournful song for the dead
sentences: The band played something between a dirge and a march, and nobody knew when to stand.
His victory speech had the cadence of a dirge, which the polls had predicted.

disabuse.definition: to free someone from a mistaken belief
sentences: Allow me to disabuse you of the notion that anyone reads the terms.
One week on the ward disabused him of every idea medical school had installed.
A disaffected faction leaked the memo and the leadership never recovered.
Disaffected voters do not switch sides; they stay home, which is worse.
Public disapprobation did more than any fine could have.
She met his explanation with silent disapprobation, which lasted the whole drive home.
It is hard to discern a pattern in four data points and very easy to invent one.
She discerned the forgery from the ink, not the brushwork.

discernible.definition: able to be perceived or recognized
sentences: There was no discernible difference between the two batches, which ended the lawsuit.
A faint but discernible improvement showed up in the third month.
A discerning reader will notice the second narrator halfway through chapter two.
"For the discerning buyer" is what catalogues say instead of "expensive."
One quiet question discomfited a speaker who had handled forty loud ones.
Discomfit once meant to defeat in battle, which explains its force.
There was a discomfiting pause before anyone agreed with him.
The most discomfiting reviews are the accurate ones.
It disconcerted him that the audience laughed in the wrong place and kept laughing.
Nothing disconcerts a liar like being asked to repeat the story backwards.

disconsolate.definition: unable to be comforted; deeply unhappy
sentences: The disconsolate team sat in the changing room for an hour without speaking.
He was disconsolate over a dog and composed at his own diagnosis.
Discord over one paragraph delayed a treaty for eleven months.
The apple of discord started a war, which is a lot to ask of fruit.
A discordant note in the third movement was, the composer insisted, deliberate.
The one discordant voice in the meeting turned out to be right.

discount.definition: to disregard or treat as unimportant
sentences: Investors discounted the warning because the warner had been early twice before.
Discount the first review and the last; the middle ones are usually honest.
Public discourse improved briefly when the comment section broke.
His discourse on bees lasted ninety minutes and converted three people to beekeeping.

discredit.definition: to damage the reputation or believability of
sentences: Rather than answer the study, they set out to discredit its author.
One fabricated detail discredited an otherwise accurate account.
A discreet cough from the doorway ended the argument instantly.
Discreet keeps the secret; discrete keeps things separate. The extra E hides.

discrepancy.definition: an inconsistency between facts or figures
sentences: A four-pound discrepancy in the accounts uncovered a decade of theft.
The discrepancy between the brochure and the building was visible from the road.
The process has four discrete stages, and everybody skips the second.
Digital means discrete: steps, not slopes.

discretion.definition: freedom to decide; good judgment in conduct
sentences: The fine is at the officer's discretion, which is another way of saying it depends.
Discretion is the better part of valor, said a character who was pretending to be dead.
The discretionary fund paid for whatever the director found interesting that year.
Discretionary spending is the first thing cut and the last thing missed.
The ear can discriminate between two notes a fraction apart and cannot describe how.
The same word covers fine judgment and gross injustice, which is a lesson in itself.
A discriminating palate can be a curse in an airport.
She was discriminating about books and cheerfully indiscriminate about films.

discursive.definition: rambling; moving from topic to topic
sentences: His discursive lectures wandered for an hour and landed, always, exactly on time.
A discursive footnote can be the best part of a dull book.

disdain.definition: contempt for something regarded as unworthy
sentences: Her disdain for small talk was legendary and slightly performative.
He looked at the spreadsheet with the disdain of a man who preferred paper.

disembark.definition: to go ashore from a ship or leave a vehicle
sentences: Four hundred passengers disembarked into a port with two taxis.
They disembarked at dawn and were lost by breakfast.

disenfranchise.definition: to deprive of a right, especially voting
sentences: The new rule disenfranchised thousands who owned no photo identification.
To disenfranchise quietly is easier than to argue openly.

disentangle.definition: to free from complication or knots
sentences: It took two accountants a month to disentangle the accounts from the excuses.
She disentangled the necklace and, in the same evening, herself from the engagement.

disgorge.definition: to discharge or give up unwillingly
sentences: The court ordered the bank to disgorge profits earned from the scheme.
The stadium disgorged sixty thousand people into a street built for two hundred.
Disheartened by the third rejection, he sent it to a fourth publisher out of spite.
The team looked disheartened at halftime and unrecognizable after it.

disillusion.definition: to free from a pleasant but false belief
sentences: A summer in the industry disillusioned her and improved her writing enormously.
Nobody thanks you for disillusioning them, however accurate you were.
It is disingenuous to call it a consultation when the decision was printed already.
The disingenuous apology apologized for the reaction, not the act.
Judicial disinterest is a requirement, not a personality trait.
The word is being lost to "boredom," and English is worse for it.

disinterested.definition: impartial; not influenced by personal stake
sentences: They needed a disinterested party, which ruled out everyone in the building.
Disinterested means fair; uninterested means asleep.
The disjointed testimony improved once the witness was allowed to sit down.
A disjointed film can be forgiven if any single scene is unforgettable.

dismiss.definition: to reject as unworthy of consideration
sentences: He dismissed the objection in a sentence and spent two years answering it.
The court dismissed the case; the newspapers did not.

disparage.definition: to belittle or speak slightingly of
sentences: He disparaged the method until his own results depended on it.
To disparage a rival's work is to advertise that you have read it.
The book joins disparate fields with a confidence no specialist would risk.
Two disparate datasets were merged, and the result meant nothing at all.

dispassionate.definition: calm and free of emotion or bias
sentences: A dispassionate account of the riot was published, and both sides called it hostile.
Dispassionate does not mean uncaring; it means the caring is not driving.

dispatch.definition: to send off promptly; to deal with quickly
sentences: She dispatched the correspondence in an hour and the difficult call in nine minutes.
The messenger was dispatched at dawn and arrived after the surrender.
A papal dispensation permitted the marriage and started a national schism.
He received a special dispensation to submit late, which everyone then requested.
The machine dispensed coffee, tea, and a liquid the label declined to name.
Let us dispense with the introductions and get to the disagreement.
The crowd dispersed after the rain arrived, having outlasted every argument.
Seeds disperse by wind, water, and the reliable carelessness of birds.
The team is dispersed across four time zones and meets, unhappily, at seven.
Dispersed populations preserve dialects that cities flatten in a generation.
Otters disport themselves in the current while everyone else works.
The word gave us "sport" after losing its first syllable somewhere in the fifteenth century.

disposition.definition: a person's usual temperament; an arrangement
sentences: A sunny disposition survives most things except an open-plan office.
The disposition of the troops was clever; the timing was not.
The most disquieting detail was how normal the office looked afterward.
A disquieting silence followed the question and answered it.

disquisition.definition: a long, formal discussion of a subject
sentences: His disquisition on medieval taxation lasted two hours and converted nobody.
The email opened with a disquisition and closed without a request.
Disregard the previous email, said the email that made everything worse.
He disregarded the warning label and became a statistic in someone's presentation.

dissemble.definition: to conceal one's true motives or feelings
sentences: He dissembled beautifully for an hour and gave himself away with a receipt.
To dissemble is to lie with your face rather than your words.

dissembler.definition: one who conceals true feelings or motives
sentences: The dissembler agreed with everyone in the room and reported all of them.
Every good dissembler is eventually undone by someone with a long memory.
The findings were disseminated by press release before the reviewers had finished.
The Latin root is sowing seed, which is optimistic about what gets spread online.
Her dissent ran twelve pages and became law twenty years later.
A body that tolerates no dissent will hear no warning either.
The dissident's essays circulated in carbon copies and outlasted the regime.
Yesterday's dissident is often on the next generation's stamps.
She dissimulated her disappointment so well that they offered her the job again.
Simulate is showing what isn't there; dissimulate is hiding what is.

dissipate.definition: to scatter and disappear; to squander
sentences: The tension dissipated the moment somebody laughed.
He dissipated a fortune in nine years and described each one as an investment.

dissolution.definition: the formal ending or breaking up of something
sentences: The dissolution of the partnership took longer than its entire productive life.
Parliament's dissolution sends everyone home to campaign for their own jobs.
Cognitive dissonance is what happens when belief and evidence share a room.
The dissonance in the opening bars was scandalous in 1913 and is a ringtone now.

distaff.definition: relating to women or the female side
sentences: The estate passed down the distaff line, which the lawyers found unusually complicated.
A distaff held wool for spinning, and the word came to stand for the women who held it.

distend.definition: to swell or expand from internal pressure
sentences: The balloon distended until the room went quiet in anticipation.
The budget distended year by year without ever being formally increased.

distill.definition: to extract the essential meaning of
sentences: He distilled forty pages into one paragraph and lost nothing but the throat-clearing.
Whiskey is distilled; so, occasionally, is wisdom, and both take years.

distinction.definition: a difference; or excellence and honor
sentences: The distinction between the two policies fits inside a comma.
She graduated with distinction and no idea what to do next.

distort.definition: to twist out of true shape or meaning
sentences: The headline distorted a careful finding into a confident prediction.
Heat distorted the rails, and the timetable followed.

distraught.definition: deeply agitated with worry or grief
sentences: The distraught owner searched three streets calling a cat that was asleep upstairs.
He was distraught for a week and functional throughout, which fooled everyone.
Distressed assets are bought by people who can afford to wait.
She sounded distressed on the phone and perfectly calm in person.
They dithered over the offer until it expired, which counted as a decision.
He dithered about the color for a month and painted it white.

diurnal.definition: occurring in the daytime or daily
sentences: Diurnal animals are simply the ones we happen to have met.
The diurnal rhythm of the office is coffee, complaint, and a brief burst of work.

diverge.definition: to move or differ in different directions
sentences: Their accounts diverge at exactly the point where the money moved.
Two roads diverged, and the poem has been misread ever since.
Two divergent interpretations of the same clause reached opposite courts.
Divergent thinking generates options; someone else has to close the list.
A diversified portfolio is an admission that nobody knows which one will fail.
The diversified farm survived the year that ruined the specialists.
Funds were diverted to a project nobody could later name.
The magician diverted four hundred people with one hand while working with the other.

divest.definition: to rid oneself of; to sell off
sentences: The university divested from coal in 2018 and from the debate immediately after.
He divested himself of the title, the office, and every responsibility except the parking space.

divine.definition: to discover by intuition or guesswork
sentences: From two sentences of the memo she divined the entire reorganization.
Water diviners hold a stick and, reliably, find water where water usually is.
The proposal was divorced from any budget anyone recognized.
His theory is elegant and entirely divorced from what happens in a kitchen.
He would not divulge the source and spent eleven weeks in a cell for it.
The letter divulged nothing and implied a great deal.
The docile horse became a different animal at the sound of a plastic bag.
A docile committee approves everything and notices nothing.

doctrinaire.definition: rigidly attached to a theory regardless of practicality
sentences: The doctrinaire approach worked in the model and starved the actual town.
He was doctrinaire in print and remarkably practical at home.

document.definition: to record in detail with evidence
sentences: She documented every conversation, which is why she still has a career.
The species was documented once, in 1904, by someone who lost the specimen.

documentary.definition: based on documents or factual record
sentences: The claim has no documentary support beyond a photograph of a photograph.
Documentary evidence beats confident memory in every courtroom on earth.

doff.definition: to take off, especially a hat
sentences: He doffed his cap to the funeral procession and put it back on, carefully.
Doff is "do off" and don is "do on" — English at its laziest and most efficient.
The rumor dogged him through three jobs and two countries.
Injuries dogged the season from the second week onward.
Dogged reporting over four years brought down a minister and a filing system.
Dogged persistence is talent's most reliable substitute.
The card contained six lines of doggerel and one genuinely moving postscript.
Doggerel survives longer than good poetry because it is easier to remember.

dogma.definition: a principle laid down as unquestionably true
sentences: What began as a working hypothesis had hardened into dogma by the third edition.
Dogma is a belief that has stopped taking questions.
He was dogmatic about grammar and cheerfully vague about everything expensive.
The most dogmatic voice in the room is rarely the best informed.
The dog's doleful expression secured a second dinner within minutes.
A doleful trumpet at a wedding suggested the band had opinions.
The dolorous bells rang for an hour, which was three minutes of dignity and fifty-seven of noise.
Her dolorous letters improved dramatically after she got a dog.
The volcano is dormant, a word geologists use to mean "not today."
The dispute lay dormant for eight years and resumed at exactly the same sentence.

dormer.definition: a window projecting from a sloping roof
sentences: Two dormers turned an attic into a bedroom and doubled the house's price.
Dormer comes from sleeping: the window belongs to a bedroom by definition.
In his dotage he confused decades but recited the entire Aeneid.
The family called it dotage; the doctors used a longer word and a worse prognosis.
She doted on the youngest and was fair to the rest, which nobody believed.
They doted on the cat with a devotion the cat received as its due.
